hops.title: Point at it: a robin's hidden ears
hops.text: Stay within reach of your child and look for a robin from where you're sitting. Ask, "Can you find its ears?" A cat has ear flaps that stick out. A robin doesn't. Feathers hide the openings to its ears. Each ear still has outer, middle and inner parts.

sources.citation: Marquette University Speech and Signal Processing Laboratory, 'Birds'
Naturalis Biodiversity Center, Bird Skin Reference glossary, 'ear' (outer ear covered by feathers)

image.caption: A robin hears without ear flaps. Feathers hide the openings to its ears.

hops.afterHeading: Questions to ask while you do it
hops.title: Ask it: whose ears would you borrow?
hops.text: After the walk, try asking, "If you could borrow any animal's ears for a day, whose would you pick, and what would you listen for?" Expect floppy bunny ears, giant elephant ears, even spinning robot ears. Cheer every design, then ask, "Which way would you point them?" There is no wrong answer here.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A child and parent seen from behind sitting on a blanket in a yard, the child holding both hands up beside their head like pretend animal ears.
image.caption: A child's own hands make the first pair of pretend animal ears.

hops.title: Say it: bush crickets hear with their front legs
hops.text: Try this: "Guess where a bush cricket keeps its ears? Not on its head. Right on its front legs! And many grasshoppers have ears on the sides of their bellies." Use it when you listen for bugs outside together, or whenever your child says every animal hears just like us.

sources.citation: Celiker E, Jonsson T, Montealegre-Z F. Biophysical Journal (2020), 118(2):464-475, PMID 31874708
University of Colorado Boulder, Colorado Arts & Sciences Magazine, 'Ancient fossils shed light on insects' hearing'
PubMed Central article PMC7532154 on the evolution of hearing organs in crickets, katydids and grasshoppers (Orthoptera)

audio.title: Three ways to talk about ears on your listening walk
audio.transcript: Hi there. Before you and your child head out for the listening walk, here are three easy ways to chat about ears along the way. First, a silly fact that kids love to repeat. When you hear chirps in the grass, ask, "Guess where a bush cricket keeps its ears? Not on its head. Right on its front legs!" Then add the bonus: many grasshoppers have ears on the sides of their bellies. It is a playful way to show that animals do not all hear the way people do. Second, look for a bird. Stay close enough to touch your child. From where you're sitting, look for a robin or a sparrow. Ask your child to find its ears. They will hunt and hunt and not see any flaps at all. Unlike cats, dogs and people, birds have no outer ear flap sticking out. Feathers usually hide the ear openings. Birds still have outer, middle and inner ear parts. Third, when the walk is over, try a dreaming question. Ask, "If you could borrow any animal's ears for a day, whose would you pick, and what would you listen for?" You might hear about floppy bunny ears, huge elephant ears, or ears that spin like a robot's. Cheer every idea, and then ask which way they would point them. There is no wrong answer, and you may get a wonderful drawing out of it. None of these need to be a quiz. Toss out a funny bug fact, a quick bird hunt or a big question, and let your child lead the noticing.
